record.paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
record.original_question: What microscopic mechanism determines the collective mass along a large-amplitude collective path, in particular how do pairing correlations, repeated level crossings near the Fermi surface, nucleon-pair hopping, and smooth changes of single-particle wave functions combine to set the inertia against changing the collective coordinate?

evidence.quote: What is the microscopic mechanism of determining the collective mass ? This is one of the central questions in our study of many-body dynamics of the LACM.
To deepen our understanding of the collective mass of LACM, it is desirable to make a comprehensive analysis of the microscopic mechanism determining it.

artifact.status_search_result: The microscopic determination of the collective mass for large-amplitude collective motion remains an active research problem in nuclear structure theory. Cranking/Inglis–Belyaev and ASCC-based estimates of M(q) are known to disagree (often by factors of 1.3–1.5), and the precise interplay of pairing, level crossings, pair hopping, and wave-function evolution continues to be studied via ASCC, GCM, and TDHFB approaches without a fully settled answer.

status_evidence.title: Adiabatic Self-Consistent Collective Coordinate method (review)
status_evidence.snippet: Microscopic derivation of collective inertia (mass) for large-amplitude collective motion and the role of pairing remain under active investigation.
status_evidence.claim: The microscopic origin of the collective mass and the contributions of pairing and level crossings are still being analyzed and refined.

status_evidence.title: Nakatsukasa et al., Time-dependent density-functional description of nuclear dynamics
status_evidence.snippet: Different prescriptions (cranking vs ASCC/GCM) give substantially different collective masses; consistent microscopic evaluation is an open issue.
status_evidence.claim: Discrepancies among microscopic prescriptions for M(q) indicate the problem is not settled.
